intro: “Emerson” is the first movement of Ives’s Piano Sonata No. 2, “Concord, Mass., 1840–60”, and is his portrait of Emerson. Ives set out seven themes on the first page and developed them through the movement, in which Beethoven’s four-note motif returns repeatedly.

sections.label: Intro · Seven themes, solo piano
sections.mNote: Short phrases overlap; each enters before the previous one ends.

sections.label: A · Lyrical verse theme, piano
sections.mNote: A lyrical theme builds to the Beethoven climax.

sections.label: B · Beethoven motif within piano chords
sections.mNote: The repeated-note figure sounds through the louder writing.

sections.label: C · High melody over rising bass
sections.mNote: The descending tune gains notes with each repetition.

sections.label: D · Song theme treated as fugue
sections.mNote: Emerson phrase leads into contrapuntal piano lines.

sections.label: E · Return of earlier piano phrases
sections.mNote: The opening episodes lead to another Beethoven climax.

sections.label: Coda · Beethoven echoes in distant keys
sections.mNote: A major and E♭ major both sound in the quiet ending.

cues.title: Seven themes, opening page
cues.text: Seven themes appear on the opening page, some only a few notes long. They interrupt and overlap in the piano, and they include fragments of the melody that returns plainly in The Alcotts.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, “Emerson”: seven overlapping themes on the first page and fragments of the cyclic melody. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Ives on Emerson and Thoreau
cues.text: At the opening of his Essays Before a Sonata, Ives called the first and last movements, Emerson and Thoreau, “composite pictures or impressions”. They give no programme of either man’s life or of any one of his works.
cues.evidence: Charles Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), introductory note on the four movements. https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm

cues.title: Copies sent out, January 1921
cues.text: In January 1921 Ives mailed two hundred copies of the Concord Sonata, with a book of essays, to people in the music world. He had paid for the printing himself. Ives was an insurance executive.
cues.evidence: Gann’s introductory account and chronology: printing at Ives’s expense in 1920, score and essays circulated in January 1921. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Human faith melody, both halves combined
cues.text: After the opening page the dynamic drops, and both halves of the sonata’s main tune sound together. The right hand plays the first half, varied, in C, and the left hand plays the second in A♭. Ives called the tune the “human faith melody”.
cues.evidence: Kyle Gann, “Following the Concord Sonata”, “Emerson”: the two halves of the human faith melody played at once in different keys once the first page quietens. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Unfinished Emerson Concerto, 1910–11
cues.text: The movement grew out of an unfinished concerto from 1910–11. In it Ives cast the soloist as Emerson and the orchestra as the crowd responding to him. In the sonata a single pianist plays both parts.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”: the unfinished Emerson Concerto and Ives’s conception of the soloist and responding masses. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Carlyle on Emerson’s paragraphs
cues.text: In his Essays Before a Sonata (1920), Ives recalled that Carlyle had told Emerson some of his paragraphs did not cohere. Ives located Emerson’s plan in “the large unity of a series of particular aspects of a subject”. Kyle Gann has written that the movement mirrors that “grand, nonlinear chaos of interrelated ideas”.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), “Emerson”, section 2: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#emerson. Gann, “Emerson”: https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Lyrical theme marked “verse”
cues.text: A lyrical theme enters in the piano. Ives labels it verse in the score, for Emerson’s poetry beside his prose. It leads to an apparent return of the opening and then a large climax based on Beethoven.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, third episode and Example 3: the score’s verse label and the subsequent false return and Beethoven climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Fugue in Four Keys, Yale
cues.text: At Yale, Ives showed Horatio Parker a Fugue in Four Keys, with all four keys sounding at once. Parker curtly asked him to bring no more such experiments. Ives turned to counterpoint, harmony and form, and in four years, Jan Swafford writes, he learned a great deal about the shaping forces of music.
cues.evidence: Jan Swafford, “Ives The Man: His Life”, Charles Ives Society: the Yale years with Horatio Parker. https://charlesives.org/ives-man-his-life

cues.title: Central episode
cues.text: A high melody descends while figures rise beneath it in the bass. The melody returns several times, with more notes and thicker chords at each return. The episode begins and ends softly, with a large crescendo between.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, central episode on score pp. 8–11 and Example 4: descending melody, rising lower patterns and progressive enlargement. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Central “nature” episode
cues.text: Kyle Gann called this central episode “nature”. The lines rising from the bass approximate a harmonic series, a common sign of nature for composers, and Emerson wrote a famous essay called Nature. The melody gains force with each repetition, a little like Ravel’s Boléro.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, central episode and Example 4. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Song episode and fugal entries
cues.text: The Emerson theme returns in a song-like passage. Fugue-like entries follow, drawn largely from the earlier verse theme, with each line beginning before the previous one has finished.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”: song-like episode after the centre, followed by fugue-like writing based largely on the verse theme. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Revisions, 1921–1947
cues.text: Ives had begun revising the sonata by 1921, and Emerson received particular attention. A substantially revised edition was printed in 1947. He went on changing the notes for more than twenty years after mailing the score.
cues.evidence: Gann’s chronology: revisions from 1921 and the new edition in print in 1947 (second edition, Arrow Music Press, later Associated Music Publishers). The recording source does not specify an edition. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Recapitulation and second C minor climax
cues.text: Music from the opening episodes returns. Beethoven’s repeated-note figure again builds to a C minor climax, the second after the large outburst in the movement’s first third.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”: late recapitulation starting with the first episode, and the two large C minor Beethoven-based climaxes. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: First performances, Cos Cob and New York
cues.text: On 28 November 1938 John Kirkpatrick played the whole sonata from memory at a private concert in Cos Cob. The public première followed at New York’s Town Hall on 20 January 1939, and the New York Tribune called it “the greatest music composed by an American”.
cues.evidence: Gann’s timeline of the sonata’s early performances, Charles Ives Society: https://charlesives.org/node/6616

cues.title: Closing section, Beethoven figure
cues.text: The Emerson theme is broken into fragments. Beethoven’s four-note figure returns in A major and E♭ major, keys a tritone apart. At the end the figure is played slowly in the low bass.
cues.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, closing paragraph: dismantled Emerson theme, Beethoven echoes in A major and E♭ major, and the final bass statement. https://charlesives.org/node/6616
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Emerson essay, closing paragraph, 1920
cues.text: Ives ended his Emerson essay with the four notes of Beethoven’s Fifth. He placed their message “above the relentlessness of fate knocking at the door”, as “the Soul of humanity knocking at the door of the Divine mysteries”.
cues.evidence: Ives, Essays Before a Sonata (1920), final paragraph of “Emerson”: https://www.gutenberg.org/files/3673/3673-h/3673-h.htm#emerson

transitions.title: Entry of the verse theme
transitions.how: The overlapping piano phrases are followed by a quiet lyrical theme, labelled verse. Its clear upper line begins another episode, which later builds to the first large C minor outburst on Beethoven’s repeated-note figure.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, third episode and Example 3: verse theme, false return and Beethoven climax. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: High melody above rising bass figures
transitions.from: B · Beethoven motif within piano chords
transitions.to: C · High melody over rising bass
transitions.how: After the Beethoven climax, a descending melody begins softly in the piano’s high register, with rising figures in the bass beneath it. The melody repeats with added notes and thicker chords. The passage forms a long arch and ends softly, at the dynamic of its opening.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, central episode, score pp. 8–11 and Example 4. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: Emerson theme returns as song
transitions.from: C · High melody over rising bass
transitions.to: D · Song theme treated as fugue
transitions.how: The repeated high melody dies away. The piano then plays the Emerson theme in a song-like version, and after it the earlier verse theme provides much of the fugue-like writing. The new lines take up tunes already heard among the louder chords.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”: central episode, subsequent Emerson-theme song and verse-theme fugue. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

transitions.title: C minor climax to distant-key echoes
transitions.from: E · Return of earlier piano phrases
transitions.to: Coda · Beethoven echoes in distant keys
transitions.how: The later Beethoven climax in C minor begins to break up. The Emerson tune breaks apart, and the repeated-note figure sounds in A major and E♭ major. These distant echoes grow quieter, and the slow final statement falls to the piano’s bass.
transitions.evidence: Gann, “Emerson”, closing account: the second C minor climax and the distant-key echoes that follow it. https://charlesives.org/node/6616

composer.epithet: Composer and New York life-insurance salesman whose music sets a hymn heard across a river against a marching band.
facts: His father George Ives; Horatio Parker at Yale, 1894–98
Church organist until 1902; insurance executive at Ives & Myrick
Concord Sonata and Essays Before a Sonata, 1920; 114 Songs, 1922
Danbury bands and hymn singing; the New England of Emerson and Thoreau
composer.background:
George Ives played his cornet across a pond so that his son could hear what distance did to the sound. He made the boy sing in one key while he accompanied in another, built instruments that could play quarter-tones and tried out the collision of two marching bands. A former Union Army bandmaster, he earned his living teaching and directing music in Danbury, Connecticut, where his son Charles was born in 1874.

The lessons also involved work. By fourteen Charles was a salaried church organist; at seventeen he wrote the Variations on America, a set of variations for keyboard on the tune of God Save the King. At Yale, which he entered in 1894, Horatio Parker taught him counterpoint, orchestration and the construction of a symphony. His First Symphony, written in a European idiom, came out of that teaching. George died of a stroke during Charles’s first term.
